title: The Discovery of Oz, the Terrible, part 4
attribution: From The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum (1900), via Project Gutenberg, in reading order.
body: “You’re more than that,” said the Scarecrow, in a grieved tone; “you’re a humbug.”
“Exactly so!” declared the little man, rubbing his hands together as if it pleased him. “I am a humbug.”
“But this is terrible,” said the Tin Woodman. “How shall I ever get my heart?”
“Or I my courage?” asked the Lion.
“Or I my brains?” wailed the Scarecrow, wiping the tears from his eyes with his coat sleeve.
“My dear friends,” said Oz, “I pray you not to speak of these little things. Think of me, and the terrible trouble I’m in at being found out.”
“Doesn’t anyone else know you’re a humbug?” asked Dorothy.

“No one knows it but you four—and myself,” replied Oz. “I have fooled everyone so long that I thought I should never be found out. It was a great mistake my ever letting you into the Throne Room. Usually I will not see even my subjects, and so they believe I am something terrible.”
“But, I don’t understand,” said Dorothy, in bewilderment. “How was it that you appeared to me as a great Head?”
“That was one of my tricks,” answered Oz. “Step this way, please, and I will tell you all about it.”

He led the way to a small chamber in the rear of the Throne Room, and they all followed him. He pointed to one corner, in which lay the great Head, made out of many thicknesses of paper, and with a carefully painted face.
“This I hung from the ceiling by a wire,” said Oz. “I stood behind the screen and pulled a thread, to make the eyes move and the mouth open.”
“But how about the voice?” she inquired.

“Oh, I am a ventriloquist,” said the little man. “I can throw the sound of my voice wherever I wish, so that you thought it was coming out of the Head. Here are the other things I used to deceive you.” He showed the Scarecrow the dress and the mask he had worn when he seemed to be the lovely Lady. And the Tin Woodman saw that his terrible Beast was nothing but a lot of skins, sewn together, with slats to keep their sides out. As for the Ball of Fire, the false Wizard had hung that also from the ceiling. It was really a ball of cotton, but when oil was poured upon it the ball burned fiercely.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Scarecrow call Oz?
options: A humbug
A coward
A thief
A wizard still

questions.prompt: Per the passage, who knows that Oz is a humbug?
options: Only the four travellers and himself
Everyone in the Emerald City
The green girl and the soldier
The Witches of the four countries

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the great Head made of?
options: Many thicknesses of paper, with a painted face
Carved green marble set with emeralds
Skins sewn together over wooden slats
A ball of cotton soaked in oil

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what was the terrible Beast really?
options: Skins sewn together, with slats inside them
A hanging Head worked by hidden threads
A costume of green silk gauze and a mask
A ball of cotton hung from the ceiling

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what made the Ball of Fire burn?
options: Oil poured on a ball of cotton
A lamp hidden behind the throne
A mirror that caught the sunlight
Green glass lit from below

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, how did Oz make the Head seem alive?
options: He hung it by a wire and pulled threads from behind the screen
He stood inside it and spoke through its mouth
He worked it with the help of the green girl
He used real magic on that one occasion

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, how did the voice seem to come from the Head?
options: Oz is a ventriloquist and can throw his voice
A speaking tube ran up through the wire
The dome echoed whatever he whispered
The green girl spoke from the chamber behind

options: Ever letting them into the Throne Room
Promising to send Dorothy back to Kansas
Building the Emerald City in the first place
Fighting against the Wicked Witch of the West

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does humbug mean?
options: Someone who deceives people by pretending
Someone who has lost his powers
Someone who talks too much
Someone who breaks his promises

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the passage?
options: The Wizard shows the plain machinery behind every terrible shape
The Wizard insists that his magic is real after all
The travellers forgive the Wizard and ask nothing more
The Scarecrow is given his brains at once

options: His coat sleeve
Dorothy's apron
The Lion's tail
A green handkerchief

options: The terrible trouble he is in at being found out
The long years he has ruled the city well

The journey they have just completed

options: Because he will not see even them
Because he keeps the Golden Cap
Because he built the city by magic
Because the Witches fear him

Out into the streets of the city

options: The lovely Lady
The great Head
The terrible Beast
The Ball of Fire

options: Complete confusion at what she has heard
Anger at having been tricked
Pity for the little old man
Relief that the danger is over
